name: Introduction to Business & Economics
description: A broad introduction to business concepts and economic thinking — how firms are organized, how markets work, basic financial literacy, entrepreneurship, and the global economy.

modules.title: What Is Business?
modules.objectives: Identify the three main types of business ownership (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation); describe business goals and the roles of key stakeholders.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 1: What Is Business?.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 1: What Is Business?.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Compare three real businesses (one sole proprietorship, one partnership, one corporation). For each, identify at least two stakeholders, explain how the ownership structure affects decision-making, and list one advantage and one disadvantage of the structure. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: notes, examples, evidence, calculations, sources, or analysis from the What Is Business? module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Economics Basics
modules.objectives: Define scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost; explain how these concepts drive economic decision-making; interpret a basic supply and demand graph.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 2: Economics Basics.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 2: Economics Basics.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Analyze the provided choice: Jordan can work a four-hour shift for $12 per hour or attend a free exam-review session. Identify the opportunity cost of each choice. Then use a current news example of scarcity to draw and label one supply-or-demand shift. Submit: a one-page memo or two-slide brief. Include: the graph, the assumption that causes the shift, the predicted change in equilibrium price and quantity, and one cited source. Evaluation: accurate use of scarcity and opportunity cost, a correctly labeled graph, and a justified conclusion.

modules.title: How Markets Work
modules.objectives: Explain the price mechanism and market equilibrium; differentiate types of competition; describe basic consumer behavior. Students will evaluate realistic scenarios, apply concepts to decisions, and justify recommendations with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 3: How Markets Work.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 3: How Markets Work.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics — review questions; complete the GIIS Learn Portal assignment for submitted practice.
modules.assignment: Select a product of your choice. Draw a supply-and-demand diagram for it, then describe what would happen to the equilibrium price if consumer incomes rose by 20%. Identify which type of competition (perfect, monopolistic, oligopoly, monopoly) best describes that market and justify your choice. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: notes, examples, evidence, calculations, sources, or analysis from the How Markets Work module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Business Functions
modules.objectives: Describe the four core business functions (operations, marketing, finance, HR); explain how these departments collaborate to achieve organizational goals.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 4: Business Functions.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 4: Business Functions.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Introduction to Business — review questions; complete the GIIS Learn Portal assignment for submitted practice.
modules.assignment: Pick a well-known company (e.g., Nike or Apple). For each of the four core functions, describe one decision that company might make and explain how that decision connects to the other functions. Present your findings in a one-page written summary or a diagram. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: notes, examples, evidence, calculations, sources, or analysis from the Business Functions module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Entrepreneurship
modules.objectives: Define entrepreneurship and identify what entrepreneurs do; explain how to identify a market opportunity; weigh the risks and rewards of starting a business.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 5: Entrepreneurship.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Entrepreneurship — review questions; complete the GIIS Learn Portal assignment for submitted practice.
modules.assignment: Brainstorm a simple business idea that solves a problem you have noticed in your school or community. Identify the target customer, the key value you offer, two major risks, and one potential reward. Write a one-paragraph executive summary of your concept. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: notes, examples, evidence, calculations, sources, or analysis from the Entrepreneurship module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Money & Banking
modules.objectives: Explain the three functions of money; distinguish checking from savings accounts; define interest and explain how banks operate. Students will evaluate realistic scenarios, apply concepts to decisions, and justify recommendations with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 6: Money & Banking.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 6: Money & Banking.
modules.practiceNote: Federal Reserve Education — classroom resources; complete the GIIS Learn Portal assignment for submitted practice.
modules.assignment: Compare a checking account and a savings account using current public terms from two financial institutions. Use a fictional $1,000 balance; do not submit account numbers or personal banking information. Submit: a comparison table and a 150-word recommendation. Include: annual percentage yield, minimum balance, one fee or fee-waiver condition, the date checked, and a simple-interest estimate clearly labeled as an estimate. Evaluation: accurate calculations, traceable sources, and a recommendation that follows from the evidence.

modules.title: Personal Finance
modules.objectives: Create a simple budget; distinguish income from expenses and needs from wants; set a short-term and long-term saving goal. Students will evaluate realistic scenarios, apply concepts to decisions, and justify recommendations with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 7: Personal Finance.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 7: Personal Finance.
modules.video2Note: TED-Ed — How to Build Good Financial Habits
modules.practiceNote: Investor.gov — review investor education topics; complete the GIIS Learn Portal assignment for submitted practice.
modules.assignment: Build a monthly budget for a fictional 18-year-old with a part-time job earning $800/month. List all expenses, categorize each as a need or a want, and show whether the budget is balanced. Then set one short-term saving goal (under 6 months) and one long-term goal (1+ year). Submit your work as a labeled business artifact that includes: (1) at least three specific examples, data points, or scenario details, (2) a table, memo, or decision matrix where appropriate, (3) a short justification for your recommendation, and (4) a 100-word reflection connecting the concept to a real company, market, workplace, or consumer decision. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: notes, examples, evidence, calculations, sources, or analysis from the Personal Finance module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Business Finance
modules.objectives: Define revenue, costs, profit, and loss; calculate break-even point; read a simplified income statement. Students will evaluate realistic scenarios, apply concepts to decisions, and justify recommendations with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 8: Business Finance.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 8: Business Finance.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Introduction to Business — review questions; complete the GIIS Learn Portal assignment for submitted practice.
modules.assignment: A small bakery sells cupcakes for $3 each. Fixed costs are $600/month; variable cost is $1 per cupcake. Calculate the break-even quantity. Then construct a simple income statement for a month in which the bakery sells 500 cupcakes. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: notes, examples, evidence, calculations, sources, or analysis from the Business Finance module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

questions.question: Which type of business is owned and operated by a single person who is personally liable for all debts?
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship has one owner who retains all profits but also bears unlimited personal liability for business debts.

questions.question: The concept that choosing one option means giving up the next best alternative is called:
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative foregone when a choice is made.

questions.question: At market equilibrium, which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, clearing the market.

questions.question: Which business function is primarily responsible for attracting and retaining employees?
options: A person who organizes resources to create a new business and accepts risk for potential reward
Resources are limited while human wants are unlimited
Specialize in wine production and trade for other goods
questions.explanation: Human Resources recruits, develops, and retains employees; the other core functions focus on operations, customers, or financial resources.

questions.question: An entrepreneur identifies an unmet customer need and builds a product to fill it. This is best described as:
questions.explanation: Recognizing an unmet need and creating a product or service to address it is the core of identifying a market opportunity.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of money?
questions.explanation: Money's three functions are medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value.

questions.question: If monthly income is $1,200 and monthly expenses are $950, the budget is:
questions.explanation: Income exceeds expenses by $250 ($1,200 − $950), so the budget has a $250 surplus.

questions.question: A company sells 400 units at $10 each and has total costs of $3,200. What is its profit?
options: Fixed costs are recovered and profit begins
Total money earned from sales before any costs are deducted
questions.explanation: Revenue is 400 × $10 = $4,000; profit equals revenue minus total costs, so $4,000 − $3,200 = $800.

questions.question: A marketing forecast predicts higher demand next month. Which business function should use that forecast to plan output?
questions.explanation: Operations uses demand forecasts to plan production capacity and inventory so the business can meet expected sales.

questions.question: Which decision best shows coordination between finance and operations?
options: Finance compares the cost of adding production capacity before operations expands
Marketing changes the company name alone
questions.answer: Finance compares the cost of adding production capacity before operations expands
questions.explanation: Finance evaluates cost and funding while operations evaluates capacity, so the two functions must coordinate before expansion.

questions.question: The break-even point is the level of sales at which:
options: Fixed costs are recovered and profit begins
questions.explanation: At break-even, total revenue = total costs, meaning the business has neither profit nor loss.

questions.question: In a basic comparison, which account is generally designed to earn more interest while limiting transaction access?
options: The interest rate set by a central bank
questions.explanation: Savings accounts are generally designed to earn interest and hold funds, while checking accounts emphasize frequent transactions; actual rates and terms must be compared.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a need and a want. Give one example of each and explain how distinguishing between them helps with personal budgeting.
questions.answer: A need is something essential for survival or basic functioning (e.g., food, shelter, clothing). A want is something desirable but not essential (e.g., a new video game, designer shoes). Separating needs from wants helps a person prioritize spending, ensure essential expenses are covered first, and identify areas where discretionary spending can be reduced to increase savings.
questions.explanation: Needs vs. wants is a foundational personal finance concept that guides budgeting priorities.

questions.question: A student is deciding whether to spend Saturday studying for an exam or working a 4-hour shift at a café for $10/hour. Define opportunity cost and calculate the opportunity cost of choosing to study.
questions.answer: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative foregone when a decision is made. If the student chooses to study, the opportunity cost is $40 (4 hours × $10/hour) in lost wages. The student must weigh this financial cost against the potential academic benefit of studying.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost applies to time and resources, not just money.

questions.question: Identify two key risks and two key rewards of entrepreneurship. Use a real-world example to illustrate one of the risks.
questions.answer: Risks: (1) Financial loss — the entrepreneur may lose invested capital if the business fails (e.g., many restaurants fail within the first year, causing owners to lose their savings). (2) Uncertainty of income — unlike a salaried job, entrepreneurial income is unpredictable. Rewards: (1) Potential for high profits and wealth accumulation. (2) Independence and the ability to build something meaningful. Other valid answers accepted.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurship involves trading job security for autonomy and the possibility of larger financial gains.

questions.question: Which ownership form is a legal entity separate from its owners and generally provides shareholders limited liability?
questions.explanation: A corporation is legally separate from its shareholders, whose financial exposure is generally limited to their investment.

questions.question: When the price of a good rises and quantity demanded falls, this illustrates:
questions.explanation: The law of demand states that, all else equal, quantity demanded decreases as price increases.

questions.question: A café uses its last $2,000 to buy an espresso machine instead of outdoor seating. The opportunity cost is:
options: The next-best benefit the outdoor seating would have provided
The price customers pay for coffee
questions.answer: The next-best benefit the outdoor seating would have provided
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up; here, buying the machine gives up the expected benefit from outdoor seating.

questions.question: A market with many sellers offering similar but differentiated products is best described as:
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition combines many sellers with differentiated products, unlike perfect competition with essentially identical products.

questions.question: Which action best shows a business balancing stakeholder interests?
options: Ignoring product defects to lower costs
Comparing the effects of a safety change on customers, employees, and owners
Keeping decisions secret from every stakeholder
questions.answer: Comparing the effects of a safety change on customers, employees, and owners
questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis weighs how a decision affects several groups with legitimate interests.

questions.question: Marketing forecasts higher demand next month. Which response best shows coordination with operations?
options: Operations adjusts capacity and inventory using the forecast
Marketing changes the company’s legal form
questions.answer: Operations adjusts capacity and inventory using the forecast
questions.explanation: Sales forecasts help operations plan staffing, inventory, and production capacity.

questions.question: A business plan's executive summary should:
options: Be the longest section of the plan
Provide a concise overview of the entire business concept
questions.answer: Provide a concise overview of the entire business concept
questions.explanation: The executive summary is a brief (1–2 page) overview that captures the mission, product, market, and financial highlights of the plan.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a fixed cost for a bakery?
options: Electricity used by the oven per hour
questions.explanation: Fixed costs remain constant regardless of output. Rent does not change based on how many loaves are baked.

questions.question: Which business function is primarily responsible for recruiting and training employees?
questions.explanation: Human Resources manages recruiting, onboarding, training, and employee relations, while operations, marketing, and finance have different primary responsibilities.

questions.question: When comparing two savings accounts, which combination gives the clearest evidence of likely value?
options: Annual percentage yield, fees, and balance requirements
questions.answer: Annual percentage yield, fees, and balance requirements
questions.explanation: Return and account conditions must be compared together because fees and requirements can offset interest.

questions.question: Which financial statement shows a company's revenues and expenses over a specific time period?
questions.explanation: The income statement (also called the profit and loss statement) summarizes revenues, costs, and expenses over a reporting period.

questions.question: Which evidence most strongly supports a proposed market opportunity?
options: Several target customers report an unmet need and current options do not solve it well
The product has a long name
questions.answer: Several target customers report an unmet need and current options do not solve it well
questions.explanation: A market opportunity requires evidence of a specific unmet or underserved customer need.

questions.question: Scarcity in economics means that:
options: Resources are limited relative to human wants
Resources are limited while human wants are unlimited
questions.answer: Resources are limited relative to human wants
questions.explanation: Scarcity exists because available resources are limited relative to competing human wants, so every allocation involves choices.

questions.question: Which budget item is most clearly a need for a fictional student living independently?
questions.explanation: Basic housing is necessary for safety and daily functioning; the other items are discretionary wants.

questions.question: A fictional monthly budget has $1,400 income, $1,050 needs, $200 wants, and $100 savings. What remains unallocated?
questions.explanation: $1,400 − $1,050 − $200 − $100 = $50, so $50 remains after needs, wants, and planned savings are deducted.

questions.question: Simple interest on a $500 savings deposit at a 4% annual rate for two years equals:
questions.explanation: Simple interest equals principal × annual rate × time: $500 × 0.04 × 2 = $40.

questions.question: A product sells for $20 and has a variable cost of $12. Its contribution margin per unit is:
questions.explanation: Contribution margin per unit equals price minus variable cost: $20 − $12 = $8.

questions.question: Describe two ways technology has changed a specific industry of your choice. Discuss one positive and one negative effect on workers in that industry.
questions.answer: Example (Retail): (1) E-commerce platforms allow retailers to reach global customers without physical stores, increasing revenue potential. (2) Automated checkout systems reduce labor time for routine transactions. Positive effect on workers: new roles in data analytics, logistics, and digital marketing have been created. Negative effect: cashier and in-store sales positions have been reduced or eliminated. Other industries and effects are valid.
questions.explanation: Technology creates disruption (job displacement) and opportunity (new roles and industries) simultaneously.

questions.question: A student proposes a reusable-lunch-container service. Define one target-customer segment, state one unmet need, identify one risk, and name one piece of evidence that would test demand.
questions.answer: A valid response specifies a focused group, such as students who bring lunch but lack a leakproof reusable container; connects that group to an unmet need; identifies a realistic risk such as price or cleaning logistics; and proposes evidence such as five structured customer interviews or a small preorder test.
questions.explanation: The response should connect a defined customer, need, risk, and low-cost demand test rather than assume that interest guarantees sales.

questions.question: A food truck has fixed monthly costs of $1,800 and variable costs of $4 per meal. It sells each meal for $10. Calculate the break-even quantity and explain what happens to profit if the owner sells 100 meals beyond break-even.
questions.answer: Break-even quantity = Fixed Costs / (Price − Variable Cost) = $1,800 / ($10 − $4) = $1,800 / $6 = 300 meals. If the owner sells 100 meals beyond break-even (400 total), the additional profit is 100 × $6 = $600, because fixed costs are already covered and each extra meal contributes $6 in contribution margin.
questions.explanation: Break-even analysis: Fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit. Every unit sold beyond break-even adds contribution margin directly to profit.

quizQuestions.question: Which type of business is easiest to set up but exposes the owner to unlimited personal liability?
quizQuestions.answer: Sole proprietorship
quizQuestions.explanation: A sole proprietorship is generally simple to establish, but the owner has unlimited personal liability for business debts.

quizQuestions.question: A stakeholder is best defined as:
options: A shareholder who owns more than 50% of a company
Anyone who is affected by or has an interest in a business's decisions
Only the employees of a company
The government agency that regulates a company
quizQuestions.answer: Anyone who is affected by or has an interest in a business's decisions
quizQuestions.explanation: Stakeholders include employees, customers, suppliers, communities, investors, and governments — anyone with a stake in the business.

quizQuestions.question: Which ownership form is a legal entity separate from its owners and can issue shares?
quizQuestions.answer: Corporation
quizQuestions.explanation: A corporation has a legal identity separate from its owners and may raise capital by issuing shares.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: State one common financial goal of a for-profit business and explain how it differs from a nonprofit organization’s primary mission.
quizQuestions.answer: Full credit: identifies sustainable profit as a common for-profit goal and explains that a nonprofit uses any surplus to support its mission rather than distribute profit to owners
quizQuestions.explanation: The distinction is the organization’s primary purpose and use of surplus, not whether it can earn more revenue than it spends.

quizQuestions.question: In Economics Basics, Scarcity occurs because:
options: People do not want many things
Resources are limited while human wants are unlimited
quizQuestions.answer: Resources are limited while human wants are unlimited
quizQuestions.explanation: Scarcity is the core economic problem: society has finite resources but infinite desires.

quizQuestions.question: You choose to watch a movie instead of studying. The opportunity cost is:
options: The price of the movie ticket
The time you spent watching the movie
The knowledge and grade improvement from studying
The cost of your internet subscription
quizQuestions.answer: The knowledge and grade improvement from studying
quizQuestions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you gave up — in this case, studying and its academic benefits.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following best describes the law of demand?
options: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
As price falls, quantity demanded falls
As price rises, quantity demanded falls
Supply and demand are always equal
quizQuestions.answer: As price rises, quantity demanded falls
quizQuestions.explanation: The law of demand: holding all else equal, higher prices lead to lower quantity demanded.

quizQuestions.question: If a lower-priced substitute becomes available, what is the most likely effect on demand for the original product, all else equal?
options: Quantity demanded rises along the same curve
quizQuestions.answer: Demand shifts left
quizQuestions.explanation: A more attractive substitute reduces demand for the original product, shifting its demand curve left.

quizQuestions.question: Market equilibrium occurs when:
options: Quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded
quizQuestions.answer: Quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
quizQuestions.explanation: At equilibrium the market clears — no surplus or shortage exists. The choice fits the prompt because it applies the central rule or concept from How Markets Work.

quizQuestions.question: If the price of a good is above equilibrium, which situation results?
quizQuestions.answer: Surplus
quizQuestions.explanation: Above the equilibrium price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus.

quizQuestions.question: In a perfectly competitive market, individual firms are best described as:
quizQuestions.answer: Price takers
quizQuestions.explanation: In perfect competition, many small firms sell identical products and must accept the market price — they are price takers.

quizQuestions.question: Which business function is responsible for converting inputs into finished goods or services?
quizQuestions.answer: Operations
quizQuestions.explanation: Operations management oversees the production process — transforming raw materials and labor into products or services.

quizQuestions.question: The finance department of a business is primarily responsible for:
quizQuestions.answer: Managing money, budgets, and investments
quizQuestions.explanation: Finance handles financial planning, budgeting, accounting, cash management, and investment decisions.

quizQuestions.question: Marketing and operations must work together primarily because:
options: They share the same office space
Sales forecasts from marketing inform production planning in operations
Marketing designs the products that operations sells
quizQuestions.answer: Sales forecasts from marketing inform production planning in operations
quizQuestions.explanation: Marketing data on expected demand helps operations plan production capacity and inventory levels.

quizQuestions.question: HR (Human Resources) is responsible for:
options: Recruiting, training, and managing employee relations
quizQuestions.answer: Recruiting, training, and managing employee relations
quizQuestions.explanation: HR's core functions include talent acquisition, onboarding, training, performance management, and employee welfare.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following best describes an entrepreneur?
options: A person who only invests money in existing companies
A person who organizes resources to create a new business and accepts risk for potential reward
A government official who regulates business
A senior manager at a large corporation
quizQuestions.answer: A person who organizes resources to create a new business and accepts risk for potential reward
quizQuestions.explanation: Entrepreneurs identify opportunities, gather resources, build businesses, and bear the financial and personal risk of failure.

quizQuestions.question: A market gap or opportunity exists when:
options: Consumer needs are not fully satisfied by existing products or services
A company has too much inventory
quizQuestions.answer: Consumer needs are not fully satisfied by existing products or services
quizQuestions.explanation: Entrepreneurs look for unmet or underserved needs in the market as the starting point for a new business.

quizQuestions.question: What is the main purpose of the market analysis section of a business plan?
quizQuestions.answer: Describe target customers and competitors
quizQuestions.explanation: Market analysis tests whether a defined customer need exists and how current competitors address it.

quizQuestions.question: A target customer is best described as:
options: Everyone who could possibly see an advertisement
The specific group most likely to need and buy the offering
Any company in the same industry
quizQuestions.answer: The specific group most likely to need and buy the offering
quizQuestions.explanation: Defining a target customer focuses product, pricing, and communication decisions on a specific need.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of money?
quizQuestions.answer: Source of comparative advantage
quizQuestions.explanation: The three functions of money are medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value. Comparative advantage is an economic trade concept unrelated to money's functions.

quizQuestions.question: Which type of account is best suited for everyday purchases and bill payments?
quizQuestions.answer: Checking account
quizQuestions.explanation: Checking accounts offer easy access to funds through debit cards, checks, and electronic transfers, making them ideal for daily transactions.

quizQuestions.question: Interest is best defined as:
options: The fee a bank charges for opening an account
The cost of borrowing money or the return on deposited money
The government tax on financial transactions
The minimum balance required by a bank
quizQuestions.answer: The cost of borrowing money or the return on deposited money
quizQuestions.explanation: Interest is paid by borrowers to lenders (or by banks to depositors) as compensation for the use of money over time.

quizQuestions.question: Using simple interest, how much interest does $1,000 earn in one year at 3%?
quizQuestions.explanation: Simple interest is principal × rate × time: $1,000 × 0.03 × 1 = $30, so the rate is applied once to the original principal.

quizQuestions.question: A budget is best described as:
options: A record of past spending only
A plan for how to allocate income across expenses and savings
A government document for public spending
A list of wants and needs
quizQuestions.answer: A plan for how to allocate income across expenses and savings
quizQuestions.explanation: A personal budget outlines expected income and planned expenses to guide financial decision-making.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a NEED rather than a WANT?
quizQuestions.answer: Rent or mortgage payment
quizQuestions.explanation: Housing is a basic need — essential for survival and functioning. The others are discretionary.

quizQuestions.question: A monthly plan lists $900 of income and $975 of expenses. What does it show?
quizQuestions.answer: A $75 deficit
quizQuestions.explanation: Expenses exceed income by $75 ($975 − $900), so the monthly plan has a $75 deficit that must be reduced or funded.

quizQuestions.question: In Business Finance, Revenue is best defined as:
options: The profit left after all expenses
Total money earned from sales before any costs are deducted
The total of all fixed costs
quizQuestions.answer: Total money earned from sales before any costs are deducted
quizQuestions.explanation: Revenue (also called sales or turnover) is the gross income from business activities before subtracting costs.

quizQuestions.question: A cost that changes with the level of production is called:
quizQuestions.answer: Variable cost
quizQuestions.explanation: Variable costs (e.g., raw materials, packaging) increase as production increases and decrease when output falls.

quizQuestions.question: Break-even point is calculated as:
options: Fixed Costs / Contribution Margin per Unit
quizQuestions.answer: Fixed Costs / Contribution Margin per Unit
quizQuestions.explanation: Contribution margin = Price − Variable Cost per unit. Break-even = Fixed Costs ÷ Contribution Margin.

quizQuestions.question: A product sells for $12 and has a $7 variable cost. What is its contribution margin per unit?
quizQuestions.explanation: Contribution margin equals selling price minus variable cost: $12 − $7 = $5 per unit.
